KEEP the five-stage lifecycle and extension strategies (advertising, price changes, adding value, new markets, new packaging — match the R067 list). DROP the 'design mix' (function/aesthetics/cost) — that is Edexcel-specific and not in R067. source_lesson.title: Product and the Product Life Cycle
source_lesson.description: Design mix, life-cycle phases and extension strategies that keep products competitive.
source_lesson.content_html:
What Makes a Product Stand Out?

When a business develops a product or service, it must balance three competing factors. The design mix captures this balance: every product sits somewhere in the triangle of function, aesthetics and cost. Function refers to whether the product does its job well. Aesthetics covers how it looks, feels and is experienced by the user. Cost relates to the expense of producing it and, by extension, the price charged. A product does not have to score equally on all three — a budget supermarket stacks of baked beans focuses almost entirely on low cost, while a luxury perfume brand leans heavily on aesthetics and function. The skill is in understanding which factor matters most to the target market.

Differentiation is the reason design matters. Differentiation gives customers a reason to choose one product over another. It can be achieved through design, brand identity, unique features, superior materials, or outstanding service. A business that fails to differentiate risks competing purely on price — a race to the bottom that squeezes profit margins.

Key Fact

The design mix has three elements: function (does it work?), aesthetics (does it look and feel right?) and cost (is it affordable to produce?). Businesses adjust the balance depending on their target market and competitive strategy.

The Product Life Cycle

No product sells at the same rate forever. The product life cycle maps four phases that most products move through over time. Understanding which phase a product is in helps a business decide where to invest marketing spend, when to cut prices, and when to develop something new.

At introduction, a product has just been launched. Sales are low because customers do not yet know it exists. The business spends heavily on promotion to build awareness. Costs are high relative to revenue, so the product is usually making a loss at this stage. Businesses use this phase to test the market and gather customer feedback. Not all products survive introduction — many are withdrawn quickly if demand fails to materialise.

During the growth phase, sales rise rapidly as more customers become aware of the product. Competitors begin to take notice and may launch similar products. The business is now making a profit and may widen distribution or add product variants. Promotional spend may shift from awareness-building to brand-reinforcing campaigns.

Maturity is the most profitable phase. Sales have peaked and are stable. Most customers in the target market have tried the product. Competition is fierce, so businesses compete on price, quality improvements, and promotional activity. Profit per unit may begin to fall as the market becomes saturated. This is the phase where many well-known brands sit for years — think of branded breakfast cereals or popular fizzy drinks that have been on shelves for decades.

Decline occurs when sales fall consistently. This may be caused by changing consumer tastes, new technology making the product obsolete, or more attractive competitor products entering the market. Sales and profits fall. A business must decide whether to withdraw the product, reduce its costs to maintain a small loyal customer base, or invest in an extension strategy to revive sales.

Key Fact

The four phases of the product life cycle are: introduction (high costs, low sales, often a loss), growth (rising sales, rising profit), maturity (peak sales, maximum profit, heavy competition) and decline (falling sales and profit). Cash flow varies significantly across the cycle.

Extension Strategies

Businesses rarely want a product to reach the withdrawal stage. Extension strategies are used to boost sales once a product enters maturity or starts to decline. Common approaches include:

  • New markets — selling to a different customer segment or entering overseas markets. A UK clothing brand might begin selling in Europe or Asia.
  • Product modification — updating the product with new features, improved materials or a refreshed design. A smartphone manufacturer regularly updates its flagship handset rather than launching an entirely new product.
  • Promotional campaigns — relaunching with new advertising or a celebrity endorsement to attract a fresh audience or re-engage lapsed customers.
  • Price reductions — a lower price attracts price-sensitive customers who were not willing to pay the original price, expanding the market.

Extension strategies cost money, so a business must judge whether the potential increase in revenue justifies the investment. If the product is genuinely becoming obsolete — for instance, a DVD player in a streaming era — even a large marketing budget may not revive demand. However, for brands with genuine customer loyalty, a well-timed extension strategy can add years of profitable sales.

Why Differentiation Is the Goal

Differentiation underpins every stage of the product life cycle. At introduction, a clearly differentiated product cuts through noise and attracts early adopters. During maturity, differentiation defends market share against cheaper competitors. After a successful extension strategy, differentiation helps justify a price premium rather than competing purely on cost. Businesses that treat differentiation as an afterthought tend to find themselves fighting price wars that erode profit margins and damage the brand.
source_lesson.exam_tip_html: For a 3-mark Outline question on the product life cycle, you must make two linked points in context — name a phase, explain what happens at that phase, and link it to the business in the question. A common mistake is just listing the phases without applying them. For a 9-mark Analyse in Context question, go beyond description: explain what the phase means for cash flow, marketing spend, and competitive pressure, using specific details from the case-study source. For a 12-mark Justify a Recommendation, remember that you do not need to evaluate both options equally — a fully developed case for one choice with a clear contextualised conclusion can reach the highest tier.
source_lesson.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The design mix (function, aesthetics, cost) helps a business position its product. Differentiating a product gives customers a reason to choose it over competitors and can justify a higher price.
  • The product life cycle has four phases — introduction, growth, maturity and decline — each with different sales levels, profitability and marketing priorities.
  • Extension strategies (new markets, product updates, promotions, price cuts) can delay decline, but only if the investment is justified by the likely increase in revenue.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the maturity phase of the product life cycle?
A) Sales are rising rapidly and the business is reinvesting profits into awareness campaigns
B) Sales have peaked and competition is fierce, often pushing prices down
C) The product has just launched and costs exceed revenue
D) Sales are falling and the business must decide whether to withdraw the product
practice_questions.marks: B) Sales have peaked and competition is fierce, often pushing prices down [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two elements of the design mix.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correct element, up to 2 marks:
• Function
• Aesthetics
• Cost
[Any two of the above for 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Dune & Stone is a small homeware brand based in Norwich. It has just launched a new range of handmade ceramic mugs. Outline one reason why Dune & Stone might use an extension strategy in the future.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks. Students should give a reason for using an extension strategy and develop the point in context:
• Dune & Stone may use an extension strategy when mug sales begin to decline (1 mark) because without action, revenue and profit will fall as customers switch to newer or cheaper alternatives (1 mark), leaving the business with unsold stock and wasted production capacity (1 mark).
• Award 1 mark for a relevant reason, 1 mark for development of that reason, and 1 mark for a contextual link to the scenario (homeware / small brand / customer loyalty).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the design mix can help a business differentiate its product.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks per point (statement + two expansions), maximum 6 marks. No case-study context is required.

Point 1 — Aesthetics:
A business can differentiate by prioritising aesthetics (1), making the product look and feel more appealing than rivals (1), which can justify a price premium and attract customers who are willing to pay more for an attractive design (1).

Point 2 — Function:
A business can differentiate through superior function (1), engineering the product to perform better or last longer than competitors’ versions (1), which builds customer loyalty and positive word-of-mouth that reduces future marketing costs (1).

[Only the best two points are marked. A third point earns no credit.]

practice_questions.text:
Revel Print Co. is a mid-sized greeting card company based in Edinburgh. It sells 600,000 cards per year at an average price of £3.50. The market for physical greeting cards has been in steady decline for three years. A rival company has just launched a digital card subscription service. Revel Print’s managing director is considering an extension strategy to revive sales.

Analyse how the product life cycle phase that Revel Print Co. is currently in might affect its marketing decisions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): The student identifies Revel Print as being in the decline phase and develops two or more well-connected analytical points that integrate specific contextual details (the 600,000 cards, £3.50 price, three-year decline, digital rival). Analysis shows how the decline phase affects both the marketing budget decision and the type of promotion strategy likely to succeed. A clear evaluative thread connects phase to decision.

Secure (5–7 marks): The student correctly identifies the decline phase and makes at least one analytical point linking the phase to a specific marketing decision. Context from the scenario is used but may not be embedded in every paragraph.

Developing (3–4 marks): The student describes characteristics of the decline phase correctly but the link to marketing decisions is general rather than analytical. Limited use of the numerical or business-specific details in the source.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic recall of a product life cycle phase or a generic statement about marketing with little or no contextual application.

practice_questions.text:
Revel Print Co. is considering two options to revive sales:
Option A: Redesign the cards using premium recycled materials and raise the average price to £5.00, targeting the premium gift market.
Option B: Partner with a national supermarket chain to reduce the price to £1.99 and significantly increase volume.

Justify which option you would recommend to Revel Print Co.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A clear recommendation is made and fully justified using specific details from the context (current price of £3.50, 600,000 volume, three-year decline). The student develops a coherent case for the chosen option, addresses likely drawbacks and explains why those drawbacks are manageable. The conclusion adds a new evaluative point rather than summarising earlier arguments.

Secure (7–9 marks): A recommendation is made with developed analytical reasoning using some contextual detail. One or more potential drawbacks of the chosen option are acknowledged. The conclusion is present but may restate earlier points.

Developing (4–6 marks): A recommendation is made with some reasoning, but analysis is general and context from the source is used only superficially. The student may address both options in parallel without reaching a clear justified conclusion.

Emerging (1–3 marks): A preference is stated with limited or no reasoning. No meaningful use of the contextual details provided.

glossary_terms.definition: The combination of function, aesthetics and cost that a business uses to design and position a product.
Making a product or service distinct from competitors' offerings in a way that is valued by customers.
A model showing the stages a product passes through from launch to withdrawal: introduction, growth, maturity and decline.
Actions taken by a business to extend the life of a product and prevent or slow the decline phase.
The stage of the product life cycle when sales have peaked, competition is most intense and profit per unit may begin to fall.
The stage when a product has just launched, sales are low, promotional costs are high and the business is typically making a loss.
